subject.title: You've Ruined My Evening/You've Ruined My Life
subject.author: Tom Raworth
subject.text:
i would be eight people and then the difficulties vanish
only as one i contain the complications
in a warm house roofed with the rib-cage of an elephant
i pass my grey mornings re-running the reels
and the images are the same but the emphasis shifts
the actors bow gently to me and i envy them
their repeated parts, their constant presence in that world

i would be eight people each inhabiting the others' dreams
walking through corridors of glass framed pages
telling each other the final lines of letters
picking fruit in one dream and storing it in another
only as one i contain the complications
and the images are the same, their constant presence in that world
the actors bow gently to me and envy my grey mornings
 
i would be eight people with the rib-cage of an elephant
picking fruit in a warm house above actors bowing
re-running the reels of my presence in this world
the difficulties vanish and the images are the same
eight people, glass corridors, page lines repeated
inhabiting grey mornings roofed with my complications
only as one walking gently storing my dream

title: The Man Who Wanted to Be Eight People
standfirst: Tom Raworth gave a poem about splitting into eight simultaneous selves a title that sounds like an overheard breakup line, then never explained the joke. It is exactly the kind of unexplained gap his whole working life was built around.

sections.heading: A Title With Nothing to Do With the Poem
sections.body:
"You've Ruined My Evening/You've Ruined My Life" sounds like dialogue caught mid-argument — the kind of line that belongs to a specific couple in a specific kitchen. The poem underneath it has no couple, no kitchen, and no argument. It is about wanting to be eight people at once, living in a house roofed with "the rib-cage of an elephant," watching actors bow and envying their "repeated parts, their constant presence in that world." Raworth never gestures back at the title again. The gap between the two is never closed, and the poem is better for the refusal.

What the poem does instead is build itself from a small deck of images — eight people, the elephant rib-cage, grey mornings, actors bowing, reels re-running, corridors of glass-framed pages, fruit picked and stored — and deal them out three times in three different orders. The third stanza rearranges phrases from the first almost word for word: "picking fruit in one dream and storing it in another" becomes "picking fruit in a warm house above actors bowing." The poem, in other words, is doing to its own vocabulary exactly what its speaker wants to do to himself: staying single and continuous while appearing, each time, as something rearranged.

sections.heading: A Life That Never Stayed Still
sections.body:
Thomas Moore Raworth was born in Bexleyheath, on the edge of London, on 19 July 1938, and as a teenager became one of the first patients ever to survive open-heart surgery. Between leaving school and starting university at twenty-nine, he spent thirteen years teaching himself printing while working ordinary jobs, and by the early 1960s was running it as a vocation rather than a trade: he founded the magazine *Outburst*, publishing Ed Dorn, Allen Ginsberg and LeRoi Jones, then Matrix Press, then, in 1965 with Barry Hall, Goliard Press — which put out Charles Olson's first British collection.

He put his reasoning for doing it all himself bluntly, decades later: it was, he said, [better, all told, to learn how to print your own books than let someone else fuck them up](https://newleftreview.org/sidecar/posts/making-games). He held an Irish passport from the age of fifty-two on, and financial hardship and poor health ran alongside him for most of his adult life — a poet who, on the evidence of his own account of himself, treated instability less as misfortune than as a working condition.

sections.heading: Speed, Emptiness, and the Black Mountain Line
sections.body:
Raworth's early poetry drew on the Black Mountain poets and the New York School alike, Robert Creeley and John Ashbery in particular, filtered through Dada and European Surrealism. By *Ace* in 1974 that mixture had hardened into a disjunctive style built from short, unpunctuated lines that open onto several readings at once — a style matched, in performance, by a reading voice clocked at breakneck speed, fast enough that a listener has no chance to rest on what she has just heard.

Raworth described the method behind that speed in his own terms: [my idea is to go the other way, you know. And to be completely empty and then see what sounds](https://newleftreview.org/sidecar/posts/making-games). One of his own lines states the same commitment as something closer to a vow: "i made this pact, intelligence / shall not replace intuition." "You've Ruined My Evening/You've Ruined My Life," with its images arriving too fast to fully settle before the next one crowds in, reads like that pact in practice — a poem that trusts what surfaces over what could be reasoned into place. Robert Creeley, for his part, simply called him [an extraordinary poet](https://poetryarchive.org/poet/tom-raworth/).

sections.heading: Print It Yourself, Judge It Yourself
sections.body:
Raworth's politics ran alongside his printing rather than through his poems: a committed socialist, he translated speeches by the Colombian guerrilla leader Fabio Vásquez Castaño, but resisted writing the kind of overtly "political poetry" that decides its own meaning in advance, treating that as a kind of dishonesty rather than commitment. The same resistance to being told what to think showed up in how he treated younger writers — the poet SJ Fowler has described emailing him unprompted, having Raworth actually read the work, and being invited down to talk, with the friendship that followed built less on poetry itself than on shared conversation and decency.

In 1977, after five years teaching in the United States, Raworth returned to England to spend a year as resident poet at King's College, Cambridge — a formal academic perch that sat oddly with a career built almost entirely outside institutions, on hand presses and small magazines run out of spare rooms.

sections.heading: Eight People, One Book at a Time
sections.body:
By the time Carcanet published his *Collected Poems* in 2003, a 550-page volume, Raworth had spent four decades moving through more than forty books and pamphlets, most of them set and printed by hands that included his own. The poet and critic SJ Fowler has called him [the finest British poet of his lifetime](https://www.3ammagazine.com/3am/tomraworth/), while also noting that Raworth found wider recognition in America than he ever quite did at home. Diagnosed with terminal cancer in January 2017, he wrote to friends with the same economy he brought to his lines: [it's been a decent run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Raworth). He died on 8 February 2017, aged seventy-eight.

The poem's speaker never gets to be eight people; he stays "only as one," containing the complications rather than escaping them. Across the small presses, the collaborations with musicians and painters, the readings on four continents, and the constant printing of his own work his own way, Raworth came about as close as a single working life allows to living the multiplication his poem only imagines — and, like his own speaker, did it one book, one version, at a time.
